name: Flaxseed (ground seed or linseed)
short: Case reports: severe anaphylaxis (incl. an infant); bowel blockage. Rats, pregnancy: lower birth weight; earlier carcinogen-induced breast tumours in offspring. Menopause trial: no serious events.
text: The most serious harms in the cited sources are allergic reactions to flaxseed (linseed) eaten as seed or flour, described in case reports: severe anaphylaxis in an 11-month-old infant after eating flaxseed, anaphylaxis in a 39-year-old woman after eating linseed, and facial swelling, breathing difficulty and hives in a 42-year-old woman 30 minutes after eating flaxseed flour; a case series of three people with flaxseed allergy, one with repeated episodes of anaphylaxis, noted that flaxseed is frequently omitted from ingredient labels. Two case reports, without abstracts, are titled as reports of obstructive ileus (bowel blockage) caused by a linseed bezoar (a compacted mass), one severe and one in an adolescent with anorexia. A 2025 review lists excessive consumption and possible contamination, particularly from cyanogenic glycosides, as safety concerns; in a crossover study in 12 healthy adults given foods that each contained the same amount of cyanide in this form, the peak blood cyanide level after linseed (5.7 µM) was lower than after cassava or bitter apricot kernels, which the authors attributed to delayed release of cyanide from linseed. On pregnancy, in rats a diet of 10% flaxseed during pregnancy and lactation lowered birth weight and altered the reproductive development of the offspring, and the authors suggested caution about flaxseed in pregnancy and lactation; in another rat study, flaxseed making up 5% or 10% of the mothers' diet during pregnancy or lactation shortened the time to chemically induced breast tumours in the offspring, and the 10% flaxseed diet also increased the number of tumours, with cadmium in flaxseed raised as a possible but unconfirmed cause. In humans, an analysis of 3,183 women in the Quebec Pregnancy Registry found no significant association between use of flax as a herbal product in the last two trimesters and low birth weight; the abstract does not say in what form the flax was taken. In a 6-month randomised placebo-controlled trial in 90 menopausal women, no serious treatment-related adverse events were reported with flaxseed meal or flaxseed extract, and neither had clinically important oestrogen-like effects on the womb lining or vagina. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
